title: The End of Rojava: Kurds in Northeast Syria Face an Uncertain Future Amid Integration With Damascus
author: C.P. Ward
content:

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd064d4ea-b926-49ec-808c-75850b368afd_5832x3888.jpeg)A
building in Qamishli, northeast Syria, bearing the name Kurdistan. September
9, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair.

QAMISHLI, Syria--Faded photographs of the dead line the walls of Fadia
Ismail's home in Hasake province, Syria--images of martyrs who died in the
long quest for a Kurdish homeland.

Her son's image is among them. Dalil was killed fighting ISIS in the flat
desert of Al-Omar oilfield in 2017 when he was just 29. Dalil "died for
Rojava," she said in reference to the Kurdish-led political project in
northeast Syria that gained de facto autonomy in 2012.

But now, as Syria's president pushes to integrate the Kurdish community of the
northeast into a unified Syria, the dream of Rojava as a self-governing
Kurdish state has all but come to an end.

"All of our martyrs have been betrayed. All the blood we shed and for what?"
she raged. "What did Dalil die for?"

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fJPA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc48deb0b-484b-4336-af14-108b24cfece1_5879x3919.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fJPA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc48deb0b-484b-4336-af14-108b24cfece1_5879x3919.jpeg)Fadia
Ismail sits in her home in Gerbawi, Hasakeh with her husband under framed
photos of martyrs from her family. September 9, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash
Nair.

On August 25th, the Autonomous Administration of North East Syria (AANES),
also known as Rojava, and its military component, the Kurdish-led Syrian
Democratic Forces (SDF), formally dissolved after more than a year of
negotiations between the SDF and the new Syrian government led by Ahmed al-
Sharaa. The talks ended when a surprise offensive by the government in January
forced the SDF into accepting an integration agreement into a Syrian state.
But many Kurds who spoke to Drop Site are fearful of rejoining a wider Syrian
state that had previously marginalized and discriminated against them for
decades under the Assad regime.

As the sun set on Gerbawi village in the countryside of Qamishli, Fadia and
her husband enjoyed the cool twilight air on their porch. "There is no
integration. This is the imposition of defeat," she said as she swatted at
flies landing on the brim of her teacup. "Alongside Dalil, how many other
lives were lost to capture Al-Omar oilfield? We lost it overnight."

"We have lost our chance at a better future."

## **Kurdish Women Fighters**

The SDF's fighters now serve under the new Syrian flag and the senior
leadership are to be given roles within the Syrian government. Mazloum Abdi,
the SDF's commander-in-chief, has been appointed as a special advisor to
President Al-Sharaa.

However, their female counterpart, the Women's Protection Units (YPJ), who
rose to prominence for their crucial role in the war against ISIS, are stuck
in limbo, as Syria's Ministry of Defense has refused to admit women into its
ranks. The YPJ grew to become one of Syria's most recognizable fighting
forces, drawing global attention for its all female battalions that fought the
Islamic State.

"Syrian law permits women to work in any position based on merit--except as
combatants," Mustapha Abdi, a senior member of the presidential team for the
implementation of the integration agreement, told Drop Site News. "There is to
be no female combat element within the Syrian military."

The decision has left former YPJ fighters in limbo. In Hasake's Khabour
military hospital, Isiyan, 19, was recovering from a recent surgery. In
January, with the SDF in full retreat ahead of the government's offensive,
Isiyan was ordered to get out of Raqqa, when her unit was ambushed on the road
to Kobane. "I was hit by a Kalashnikov round that shattered the bones in my
shoulder," she said. "I lost a lot of blood." She has been hospitalized since
then, her days plagued by boredom and her nights by nightmares of what
happened.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yKP3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe8d5cd8c-05e8-43f2-8fc5-f458625d888e_5886x3924.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yKP3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe8d5cd8c-05e8-43f2-8fc5-f458625d888e_5886x3924.jpeg)Isiyan,
19, recovers from a battle injury in a hospital in Hasakeh as her comrades
visit her. September 7, 2026. Photo by: Anagha Subhash Nair.

Despite the attack, she is impatient to get back to her unit. "I miss my
comrades," she said. Isolated in hospital, she seemed unaware of the SDF's
dissolution. And like the rest of the YPJ, she had no sense of what her future
would hold.

While integration into the Syrian military appears to be a red line for the
government, Ruksan Mohammed, the YPJ spokesperson, said that, following the
official dissolution of the SDF, YPJ leadership had met with officials from
the Interior Ministry, and that "the possibility of integrating the YPJ as a
special and organized force was emphasized."

"We discussed how women can play an important role in protection of rights and
society," she told Drop Site. However, "no dates have yet been set for the
upcoming meetings because we are waiting for a response from the Ministry of
Interior."

Before the dissolution of the SDF, as integration progressed in all other
dimensions, the YPJ had largely found itself frozen out of talks, and
according to Mohammed, were only afforded a single meeting with the government
in April.

Abdi confirmed this, saying that the lack of any further meetings was because
the YPJ "were offered non-combat roles, such as administrative office based
work, which they refused."

## **Violence Targeting Kurds**

The atmosphere is tense in northeast Syria following repeated incidents of
violence targeting Kurds. Last Thursday, Sipan Hazni, a recently integrated
Kurdish soldier was kidnapped and decapitated by Arab members of the Begara
tribe. His killing set off the latest round of mass unrest, culminating in a
riot and a fire at a prison in Kobane, which resulted in the deaths of seven
detainees.

In Hasake city, the government's decision to end SDF-era fuel subsidies has
left the city cloaked in darkness. "People can't afford the generator bills
now, so they leave the lights off," Musa Kiki, 65, said. "What kind of
government is this?"

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!U-6R!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a339721-1920-4d74-b6ea-
acebec4821c7_5897x3931.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!U-6R!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a339721-1920-4d74-b6ea-
acebec4821c7_5897x3931.jpeg)Internal security forces stand in Qamishli during
a protest in northeast Syria. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash
Nair.

Kiki was attacked by the people who stole his home. He was part of the first
convoy of Kurdish refugees returning to their homes in Serekaniye, a region
from which he was displaced following Operation Peace Spring, an incursion by
Turkey and the Turkish-backed Syrian National Army militia in 2019.

When he arrived back, he found his camera shop had been seized by a stranger
and people were living in his house. "Honestly, I wish I had never tried to go
back," he said, stubbing out a thin cigarette. "The house had been ransacked.
There were no windows or doors. The stairs were destroyed and someone had
ripped out all the cables."

"These people aren't even from the area," he added. "The person who took my
home is from Deir Ez Zour, and my brother's home is occupied by an Iraqi,
imagine that."

Despite the integration agreement stipulating the safe return of displaced
peoples, under the protection of the Syrian government, Kiki and a number of
other returnees were attacked by a group of armed men in the street.

"A large group of masked men came at us with clubs and knives, they were
dragging people out of their cars," he recounted. "One smashed the windshield
of our car and the glass injured my grandchild."

Ahmad Al-Hilali, the government-appointed deputy governor of Hasake, condemned
the attacks, while Mahmoud Khalil Ali, the deputy head of Hasake's internal
security forces, announced the arrest of several perpetrators.

However, the government's response did little to quell the simmering anger,
with the attack setting off a night of rioting in Hasake province, during
which protesters stormed Hasake city's internal security headquarters and
burned the recently hoisted Syrian flag. The following day, a security point
of recently integrated SDF fighters was attacked, killing one and injuring
three.

Kiki has little trust in the government. Although the occupant in his home has
assured him that he would leave once he has found an alternative place to
stay, "there is no way to ensure that," he lamented. "If the government wanted
they could go in and clear them out in a day, but they won't."

"Who can I complain to?" he added. "The government has done nothing for us."

## **Language and Kurdish Identity**

The issues at play also extend to governance and, in a crucial way, to
language.

Behind blastproof walls and multiple layers of security checks, Jihan Said
Hisam is busy in her new role as the newly appointed head of Qamishli
municipality. Until June, she had been negotiating with the government on
behalf of the AANES, until her name was suggested for the position during
talks. Now, she sits in front of a large Syrian flag speaking on behalf of
that same government.

"I am optimistic for the future," she said. "After 15 years of war, we can
begin again and rebuild Syria." Before the interview, her press office
informed Drop Site that she wouldn't be able to answer "political questions."

Not long after the meeting, last Thursday, a large column of hundreds of
children and young men and women, chanting and holding placards calling for
the protection of Kurdish language, wound its way to the gates of the
municipality building. Young boys attempted to scale the blast walls, but were
pulled down and scolded by the armed guards.

After a few minutes, to the whistles and cheers of the awaiting protesters,
Hisam made her way into the crowd to make an impromptu speech. "Although we
are having a difficult time with the government, I urge you not to stop
studying," she railed. "Your education is vital and we still believe the
government may reverse its decision."

"I stand with you completely and I will work to raise your voices with
Damascus," she added.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!psBa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7ce890d6-d3b3-40ed-918b-58564dc0f094_5559x3706.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!psBa!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7ce890d6-d3b3-40ed-918b-58564dc0f094_5559x3706.jpeg)Jihan
Said Hosam, head of the Qamishli municipality, speaks to protesters outside
her office in northeast Syria. September 10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash
Nair.

Despite the formal dissolution of the AANES, the office of the Department of
Foreign Affairs remains a beehive of activity. In a plush office inside, Ilham
Ahmed greeted a number of different officials.

Until recently, she had been the co-president of the AANES, but following the
dissolution, Ahmed is to become a member of parliament with a role on the
Constitutional Committee, responsible for overseeing the drafting of Syria's
new constitution.

"We still don't know how much power the constitutional committee will have,"
she acknowledged. "Although we expect the parliament to play the standard
legislative role in developing Syria's institutions."

While Ahmed spoke diplomatically, she admitted shortcomings in how
negotiations are unfolding. "We feel that the issues aren't really being taken
seriously," she explained. "Their approach is superficial and won't lead to
meaningful solutions."

Despite that she recognized that the government has been willing to compromise
on certain issues. "They initially offered us a deal which would have had
Kurdish offered in school as an optional second language, akin to English,"
she said. "We rejected this offer outright."

"While we ultimately seek education in Kurdish, the outline of the integration
file is yet to be finalized, so we remain optimistic," she added.

As part of the integration agreement, Kurdish--the language of education for
the last decade in northeast Syria while it was relatively autonomous--is set
to be taught for three hours a week, alongside an additional hour of
geography, history, or philosophy class in Kurdish. This is designed as a
transitional settlement during the next academic year while a final settlement
is yet to be agreed upon.

Last Wednesday, hundreds of children gathered in the streets and schoolyards
of Qamishli. They chanted in Kurdish, demanding constitutional recognition for
their language, and rejecting Damascus's plans to return northeast Syria's
education system to Arabic.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WY7f!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdf0838d2-7a22-4af1-b820-ab722eca86d9_5376x3584.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WY7f!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdf0838d2-7a22-4af1-b820-ab722eca86d9_5376x3584.jpeg)_​
​People protest in Qamishli against a decision as part of SDF-Damascus
integration that reduces the use of Kurdish language in education. September
10, 2026. Photo by Anagha Subhash Nair._

"I don't speak Arabic well. I won't be able to learn in it," said Jihan Hafer,
14. "If they make us learn in Arabic, then I won't come to school."

"I'm scared for my future, that I will lose my chance for an education."

Mustapha Abdi, a senior member of the government's negotiating team,
acknowledged that the agreed settlement didn't go far enough. "To be honest,
three classes a week is good in interior regions, but in Kurdish areas like
northeast Syria, it is not enough completely," he admitted.

He explained that while 1,400 schools are set to teach Kurdish, the government
hopes "the number can also increase in the next year."

"We have started now as a first step. We don't want to make the step too big,
so that the step succeeds," he added.

Mezkil Hassan, a lecturer in Kurdish language at Rojava University, believes
the policies are part of an effort to reverse a decade-long linguistic and
cultural renewal that has taken place amongst northeast Syria's Kurdish
population.

"The Kurdish people have learnt that their existence is connected to their
language," explained Hassan. "This decision threatens the language and
undermines Kurdish identity within Syria."

Rojava University, founded in 2016 as a Kurdish language university, and only
recently recognized by the Syrian government as part of the integration
agreement, is set to switch teaching over to Arabic according to Hassan.

The Ministry of Higher Education did not respond to a request for comment.

Many Kurds fear a return to the Assad era, in which "the state did not
recognize Kurdish identity as a legitimate part of Syrian culture," explained
Alexander McKeever, a researcher and author of the newsletter _This Week in
Northern Syria_. "It viewed the Kurds as an alien population and so banned
Kurdish-language instruction and cultural production."

The Syrian government has sought to allay these concerns. In January, Al-
Sharaa issued a presidential decree that recognized Kurdish as a "national
language," and annulled a controversial 1962 census that had effectively
stripped citizenship from thousands of Kurds.

However, this decree doesn't make Kurdish an "official" language nor one that
is constitutionally protected. In fact, Syria is yet to draft its
constitution.

Despite the formal dissolution of the SDF, northeast Syria remains in a
liminal state--not fully Syria, but not entirely separate either. The
individuals manning the checkpoints are no different than before, although
some now wear the uniform of the government. While the flag of Syria's
government flies above public buildings, it is rare in the city streets, where
the flags of Rojava and photos of martyrs remain ubiquitous.

The future of northeast Syria will not be determined by the change of flags or
uniforms. After 15 years of governing themselves, those who sought to build an
autonomous system are being asked to place their trust in a centralized state.

Whether that trust can be built will determine the success of integration and
for the Kurdish community, it may come down to whether the new government can
make them feel that there is still a place for them under Syria's new flag.

_* Baderkhan Ahmed contributed to this report._
